Title: Inconsistent file extensions between apm.yml and apm.lock.yaml
Body: ## Summary

APM currently uses:
- `apm.yml` for the manifest
- `apm.lock.yaml` for the lockfile

These two files are both YAML-based, but use different file extensions (`.yml` vs `.yaml`), which feels inconsistent.

## Problem

This inconsistency can be slightly confusing for users, especially since both files are:

- YAML 1.2 documents
- Core project configuration files
- Expected to be committed to version control

Most ecosystems tend to keep naming consistent across manifest and lockfile (e.g. `package.json` /
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
per lockfile spec).
- However, the choice of `.yaml` over `.yml`, and the inconsistency with `apm.yml`, is not explained in the current documentation.

## Question

Was this inconsistency intentional?

If not, would you consider aligning the extensions for better consistency and developer experience?

Title: [FEATURE] --update should re-resolve transitive dependency tree when content changes at the same commit
Body: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

When a package author updates the dependency tree (e.g. removes a transitive dependency) without creating a new commit on the default branch, `apm install --update` does not detect the change. It compares the `resolved_commit` in `apm.lock.yaml` against the current upstream ref — and since the commit SHA is identical, it skips re-resolution entirely. The only workaround is to delete `apm.lock.yaml` and run a fresh `apm install`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 doesn't address the root cause.
- **Upstream discipline** — requiring package authors to always create new commits for dependency tree changes. This is fragile and hard to enforce.

**Additional context**

- The lock file already stores `content_hash` per dependency, so the data needed for this check is already available.

Title: Content security scanning for prompt files (hidden Unicode detection)
Body: ## Problem

Shared prompt and instruction files (`.cursorrules`, `.github/prompts/`, etc.) are becoming a de facto supply chain — but without any integrity guarantees. Researchers [found that 6 of 50 popular shared `.cursorrules` files](https://agentseal.org/blog/cursor-rules-hidden-instructions) contained hidden zero-width Unicode characters embedded between visible text.

These characters are invisible to humans but LLMs tokenize them individually, meaning models can process instructions developers cannot see. Some had patterns consistent with deliberate instruction embedding using Unicode tag characters (U+E0001–U+E007F), which map 1:1 to invisible
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 |

### Product positioning

This is the first pillar of `apm audit`. Future modes include `--ci` (lock consistency) and `--drift` (on-disk divergence), as documented in the [governance guide](https://microsoft.github.io/apm/enterprise/governance/).

Title: Question : How to avoid duplicated AI primitives when those are present in Git repo and install in dev local computer
Body: **What I'm trying to do**

I distribute AI primitives (agents, skills, guardrails, standards) through APM. The same primitives live in their canonical Git repository and get installed onto individual developer machines when a developer runs apm install -g <package>.

**The problem**

I end up with what looks like two copies of the same primitive — one in the Git source of truth, one materialized locally. When both are present, it's unclear how the user should is supposed to treat them.

**Questions**

What's the recommended pattern to avoid the duplication in the first place ?
